passages.t: Scarecrow gods and the living God
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to the house of Israel. They must not learn the ways of the nations or be terrified by signs in the heavens (verse 2). ‘For the customs of the peoples are worthless’ (verse 3). A tree is cut down, carved by a craftsman, covered with silver and gold, and nailed down so it will not totter (verses 3 and 4). ‘Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch, their idols cannot speak. They must be carried because they cannot walk’ (verse 5). They can do no harm and no good.

‘There is none like You, O LORD. You are great, and Your name is mighty in power’ (verse 6). Who would not fear the King of nations (verse 7)? The idols are silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, dressed in blue and purple, all made by human hands (verse 9). ‘But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King’ (verse 10).

They are to say that the gods who made neither heaven nor earth will perish (verse 11). ‘The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom and stretched out the heavens by His understanding’ (verse 12). When he thunders, the waters in the heavens roar (verse 13). The idols have no breath in them (verse 14). ‘The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The idol-making of verses 3 to 5 and 9 matches what is known of ancient practice. A god's statue often had a wooden core, overlaid with beaten silver and gold, fixed to its base, and dressed in fine garments dyed blue and purple. Purple dye came from sea snails on the Phoenician coast and was among the costliest goods in the world. The scarecrow in a cucumber patch is a homely picture: a stick figure in a field, frightening birds and nothing else.

Signs in the heavens were the omens that Babylon's sky-watchers read. The nations were terrified of them. Israel need not be.

Verse 11 is written in Aramaic, not Hebrew, the only such verse in the book. Aramaic was the common language of diplomacy and trade across the empires, so the line reads like a message Israel is given to say in the nations' own tongue.

The Greek translation of Jeremiah lacks verses 6 to 8 and 10, the hymns of praise, and places verse 9 inside verse 5. Bibles in English follow the longer Hebrew text.
passages.later: A psalm mocks idols in the same way: ‘Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men’ (Psalm 115:4). Paul praises believers who ‘turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God’ (1 Thessalonians 1:9).
passages.hard:
Is it unfair to mock other people's religion as nothing but wood and metal?

The satire can sound crude, and ancient worshipers did not think the statue was simply the god; they believed a god could come to dwell in a properly dedicated image. Jeremiah likely knew that. His point is that whatever the theory, the practice ended in people bowing before an object their own hands had made, and fearing powers that could not act.

The chapter is addressed first to Israel (verse 1). Its target is God's own people borrowing a religion they had been warned against. It is a warning from inside before it is an attack on anyone else, and it gives no leave for contempt toward people of other faiths. Christians reading it have generally applied it to anything they build and then trust to save them.
passages.asks: The idols had to be carried because they could not walk. Ask what you carry, protect and keep upright that you also look to for safety. And ask what it would mean to fear the Maker of all things more than the signs and powers around you.

passages.t: Pack your bundle, and a prayer for correction with justice
passages.happening:
‘Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege’ (verse 17). God will sling out the people of the land (verse 18).

The city speaks. “Woe to me because of my brokenness; my wound is grievous!” (verse 19). Yet it says this is its sickness, and it must bear it (verse 19). ‘My tent is destroyed, and all its ropes are snapped’ (verse 20). Its sons are gone, and no one is left to pitch the tent. The shepherds have become senseless and do not seek the LORD, so the flock is scattered (verse 21). A report comes from the north, and the cities of Judah will be a haunt for jackals (verse 22).

Then a prayer. ‘I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps’ (verse 23). ‘Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice’ (verse 24), not in anger, or the people will be brought to nothing. The prayer asks God to pour out his wrath on the nations that do not know him and have devoured Jacob (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The bundle in verse 17 is the small pack an exile could carry. The people are told to get ready to leave.

The tent with snapped ropes is the old picture of home for a people whose ancestors lived in tents. Jerusalem speaks like a mother whose children are gone and who has no one left to raise her shelter.

The shepherds are the kings and leaders. They did not seek the LORD, so the flock scattered.

The last verse prays that God's anger would fall on the nations who devoured Jacob, rather than on Jacob alone. It hands judgment to God. It nearly matches a verse of Psalm 79.
passages.later: Proverbs says the same as verse 23: ‘A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps’ (Proverbs 16:9). Verse 25 is almost the words of a psalm: ‘Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You’ (Psalm 79:6).
passages.asks: The prayer asks to be corrected with justice, not destroyed in anger. Ask whether you have asked God to correct you, and what you fear in asking. And ask where you have tried to direct your own steps as if your way were your own.
